sites.name: Dan River Community Health, Main Street
Dan River Community Health, South Boston

resources.name: Southside Area Agency on Aging — Alzheimer's respite program
resources.summary: Up to 10 hours a week of in-home respite for caregivers of people with dementia; sliding scale, waitlist varies by county.

resources.name: Halifax Senior Services respite vouchers
resources.summary: Quarterly respite vouchers redeemable with approved in-home aides.

resources.name: Dan River Adult Day Center
resources.summary: Weekday adult day program with memory-care track; transport within 15 miles of Danville.

resources.name: South Boston Adult Day Health
resources.summary: Adult day health with nursing on site, Monday to Friday.

resources.name: Pittsylvania Rides (demand-response transit)
resources.summary: Door-to-door rides for medical appointments; book 48 hours ahead.

resources.name: Halifax County Medical Transport
resources.summary: Medicaid non-emergency medical transportation broker and volunteer drivers.

resources.name: Henry–Martinsville Ride Connect
resources.summary: Volunteer driver program for older adults; medical appointments prioritized.

resources.name: Meals on Wheels of Southside Virginia
resources.summary: Weekday home-delivered meals; dementia-friendly check-in at the door.

resources.name: Memory Café at Danville Public Library
resources.summary: Second Tuesday monthly; a social hour for people living with dementia and their care partners.

resources.name: Caregiver Circle — Chatham
resources.summary: Peer support group for family caregivers, evenings, with respite care on site.

resources.name: Halifax Caregiver Support Group
resources.summary: Monthly support group facilitated by a licensed counselor.

resources.name: Southside Legal Aid — advance directives clinic
resources.summary: Free help with powers of attorney, advance medical directives and Medicaid long-term-care applications.

resources.name: Piedmont Home Care Partners
resources.summary: Licensed personal-care aides; Medicaid waiver and private pay.

resources.name: Dan River Behavioral Health — caregiver counseling
resources.summary: Short-term counseling for caregivers; telehealth available.

resources.name: Mecklenburg Senior Center adult day
resources.summary: Adult day program three days a week in Boydton.

resources.name: Lake Country Rides
resources.summary: Scheduled medical transport across Mecklenburg County.

education.title: What dementia is, and what it is not
education.summary: Dementia is a group of symptoms, not one disease. Memory loss is only part of it.
education.body: Dementia means thinking skills have declined enough to get in the way of daily life. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, but there are others, and some people have more than one. It is not a normal part of getting older, and it is not the person being difficult on purpose. What changes first differs from person to person: memory, finding words, judgment, or mood. What to do: ask the clinic which type has been diagnosed and what to expect over the next year, and write the answer in your care plan.
education.source: National Institute on Aging, What Is Dementia?

education.title: How the stages are described
education.summary: Clinics use scales like CDR and FAST. Knowing the stage helps you plan, not predict.
education.body: The clinic may describe the stage with a number (CDR 0.5 to 3) or a FAST stage (1 to 7). Early stage: needs reminders and help with money and medicines. Middle stage: needs help choosing clothes, bathing, and may wander or get upset in the evening. Late stage: needs help with eating, walking, and all personal care. People move through stages at different speeds, and a sudden change usually means something else is wrong, such as an infection. What to do: if you see a sudden change over days, not months, log it and call the clinic.
education.source: Reisberg FAST staging; Morris CDR, as summarized by NIA

education.title: A steady routine lowers everyone's stress
education.summary: Same wake time, same meal times, the hardest tasks when the person is at their best.
education.body: People with dementia do better when the day is predictable. Keep wake, meal, and bed times steady. Do bathing and appointments in the morning if mornings are calmer. Offer two choices instead of open questions ("the blue shirt or the green one?"). Break tasks into one step at a time and let the person do what they still can, even if it is slower. What to do: write tomorrow's routine on a card where you both can see it.
education.source: NIA, Tips for Caregivers: Daily Care

education.title: Bathing without a fight
education.summary: Warm room, towels ready, let them hold a washcloth, and skip the full bath on hard days.
education.body: Bathing is often the biggest struggle because it is cold, confusing, and feels like a loss of privacy. Warm the bathroom first. Have everything within reach. Give the person a washcloth to hold so their hands are busy. Talk through each step before you do it. A sponge bath at the sink two or three times a week is fine on hard days. What to do: if bathing is a daily fight, tell the clinic; the occupational therapist can suggest equipment and a different approach.

education.title: Late-afternoon restlessness (sundowning)
education.summary: Confusion and agitation that gets worse as the light fades. Light, routine, and a quiet evening help.
education.body: Many people with dementia become more restless, anxious, or confused in the late afternoon and evening. Causes include tiredness, hunger, shadows, and too much going on. Turn lights on before dusk, close curtains so the windows do not reflect, keep the evening quiet, and avoid caffeine after noon. A short walk earlier in the day helps sleep. What to do: log when it starts and what was happening; patterns help the clinic suggest changes. If it is new and sudden, call the clinic, because an infection or a new medicine can cause it.
education.source: NIA, Tips for Coping with Sundowning

education.title: When the person is upset or angry
education.summary: Behavior is communication. Look for pain, need for the bathroom, fear, or too much noise.
education.body: Anger or agitation almost always has a cause the person cannot say out loud: pain, needing the toilet, being too hot or cold, hunger, fear, or a room that is too loud. Do not argue or correct. Lower your voice, slow down, step back, and change the subject or the room. Check for pain and toileting first. Never try to restrain the person. What to do: if you or the person are in danger, call 911 and tell the dispatcher the person has dementia. Otherwise log it and tell the clinic; new agitation can be a sign of a urinary infection.
education.source: NIA, Coping with Agitation and Aggression

education.title: Wandering and getting lost
education.summary: Six in ten people with dementia will wander at some point. Prepare before it happens.
education.body: Wandering can happen even in people who have never done it. Put a recent photo where you can find it fast. Register with your local sheriff's office or a medical ID program. Place locks high or low on exit doors, out of the usual line of sight. Keep car keys out of sight. A door chime tells you when a door opens. Make sure the person gets exercise and has something to do in the afternoon. What to do: if the person is missing, call 911 right away. Most are found within a mile and a half of home.

education.title: Preventing falls at home
education.summary: Remove loose rugs, light the path to the bathroom, and review medicines that cause dizziness.
education.body: Falls are the most common reason someone with dementia goes to the emergency room. Remove throw rugs and cords from walkways. Put night lights between bed and bathroom. Install grab bars by the toilet and in the shower. Have the person wear shoes with backs, not slippers. Ask the clinic to review medicines, especially sleep aids and blood pressure pills, which cause dizziness. What to do: after any fall, even without injury, log it in the app; the clinic will follow up within a day.

education.title: Keep one medicine list and bring it everywhere
education.summary: One list, every pill and supplement, updated after every visit. Connect Medicare to see what was actually filled.
education.body: Older adults with dementia often see several prescribers, and lists drift apart. Keep one list with the name, strength, how often, and why. Include over-the-counter sleep aids and supplements; diphenhydramine (in many "PM" products) can worsen confusion. If you connect Medicare records in this app, you will see what the pharmacy actually filled, which is often different from the list. What to do: bring the list to every visit and ask the clinic to go through it with you once a year or after any hospital stay.
education.source: AGS Beers Criteria (2023) summary; NIA medication safety

education.title: Your own strain is a medical issue
education.summary: Caregivers who are worn down get sick more and the person they care for lands in the hospital more. Check in every month.
education.body: Caring for someone with dementia is a job that goes on around the clock. Strain shows up as poor sleep, short temper, headaches, higher blood pressure, and losing interest in things you used to enjoy. It is not weakness and it is very common. The monthly check-in in this app (12 questions plus two about mood) exists so the clinic can see strain building and act before it becomes a crisis. What to do: do the check-in each month, see your own doctor at least once a year, and ask about respite before you feel you need it.
education.source: Zarit Burden Interview literature; NIA, Caring for Yourself

education.title: Respite: what it is and how to get it
education.summary: A break for you: a few hours at home, a day program, or a short stay. Programs exist in every pilot county.
education.body: Respite means someone else cares for the person for a while so you can rest, work, or see your own doctor. It comes as in-home aides for a few hours, adult day programs, or short overnight stays. In Southside Virginia, the Area Agency on Aging runs respite programs, some adult day centers have memory-care tracks, and Medicaid waivers can pay for in-home help. There are often waitlists, so apply early. What to do: open Help nearby, pick a respite or adult day listing, and press Contacted when you call; the clinic sees it and can help if you get stuck.
education.source: Virginia Department for Aging and Rehabilitative Services; local AAA programs

education.title: What Medicare pays for, and what it does not
education.summary: Medicare covers doctor visits and a yearly wellness visit, not long-term personal care at home. Medicaid may.
education.body: Medicare Part B covers doctor visits, the Annual Wellness Visit (which includes a cognitive check), and a care planning visit for cognitive impairment. Part D covers prescriptions. Medicare does not pay for ongoing help with bathing, dressing, or supervision at home. Virginia Medicaid's CCC Plus waiver can pay for personal care and respite if the person qualifies by income and need. People with both Medicare and Medicaid ("dual eligible") have extra help with drug costs. What to do: ask the clinic or Southside Legal Aid about a Medicaid long-term-care screening if care needs are growing.
education.source: CMS, Medicare & You; Virginia DMAS CCC Plus

education.title: Papers to get in place while the person can still decide
education.summary: A health care power of attorney and an advance directive, signed early, save hard decisions later.
education.body: While the person can still understand and express wishes, get two documents: a durable power of attorney for health care (who decides when they cannot) and an advance medical directive (what they want). Virginia's forms are free and do not need a lawyer, though legal aid will help. Keep copies with the clinic and in the app. Also talk about who will handle money and bills. What to do: contact the advance directives clinic under Help nearby; bring the signed power of attorney to the clinic so it can be recorded with your representative confirmation.
education.source: Virginia Advance Medical Directive (Va. Code § 54.1-2984); NIA, Legal and Financial Planning

education.title: If the person goes to the emergency room
education.summary: Bring the medicine list and the care plan. Tell every nurse about the dementia. Call the clinic the next day.
education.body: Hospitals are confusing and often make dementia symptoms worse for a time. Bring the one-page care plan from this app and the medicine list. Tell every new nurse and doctor that the person has dementia and how they usually communicate. Stay if you can; a familiar face prevents delirium. Ask what changed in the medicines before you leave. What to do: log the visit in the app; the clinic will call within two days to go over medicines and what happened.
education.source: NIA, Going to the Hospital: Tips for Dementia Caregivers
